entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: At the most central and important part of something, such as a problem, a debate or an organization.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, speeches and serious discussion, and also in conversation. It often follows *be* or *lie* (*Money lies at the heart of most family fights*) or starts a sentence with inverted word order: *At the heart of the problem is a lack of trust.* It sounds a little more vivid than *the main point*.
entries.pattern: be / lie at the heart of something; At the heart of X is Y
examples: **At the heart of** the argument was a simple question: who would pay for the repairs?
Money lies **at the heart of** most fights between siblings over a parent's house.
Fresh, local ingredients are **at the heart of** everything this restaurant does.

drill.sentence: My grandmother used to say that trust is {{at the heart of}} any good marriage.
drill.hint: at the very center of (not *at the core …* or *at the root …*)

entries.related: *at the core of* — very similar; *at the root of* — at the original cause of a problem; *the crux of the matter* — the most important or difficult point.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: More complicated, interesting or important than it first seems.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, reviews and journalism, usually as *there's more to someone / something than meets the eye*. It suggests a hidden side, either positive (a hidden talent or depth) or suspicious (a hidden motive). It also works without *to*: *There's more going on here than meets the eye.*
entries.pattern: there's more to someone / something than meets the eye
examples: The quiet new kid in class is a chess champion — there's **more to him than meets the eye**.
The company's sudden sale of its headquarters suggests there's **more** going on **than meets the eye**.
There's a lot **more** to making a good croissant **than meets the eye**.

drill.sentence: The old farmhouse looked ordinary, but there was {{more to it than meets the eye}}: a hidden cellar full of old letters.
drill.hint: a hidden side not visible at first — a vision phrase

entries.related: *hidden depths* — unexpected qualities in a person; *don't judge a book by its cover* — don't judge by appearance; *the tip of the iceberg* — a small visible part of a much bigger problem.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To work out the truth from the facts or clues you have, especially when the conclusion is fairly obvious.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and storytelling, often about discovering a secret: *She put two and two together.* It suggests a simple, logical step rather than clever detective work. The joking extension *put two and two together and get five* means reaching a wrong conclusion.
examples: When I saw the empty cookie jar and the crumbs on my son's shirt, I **put two and two together**.
Nobody told the neighbors about the divorce, but they **put two and two together** when only one car stayed in the driveway.
Investors **put two and two together** after the CEO quietly sold half his shares.

drill.sentence: My sister kept leaving the room to take calls and smiling at her phone, and it didn't take long to {{put two and two together}}: she had a new boyfriend.
drill.hint: work it out from the clues — an arithmetic image (not *connect the dots*)

entries.related: *connect the dots* — see how separate facts fit together; *figure something out* — plainer; *read between the lines* — understand a hidden meaning.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To deal with or understand only a small part of a subject or problem, while much more remains.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, journalism and talks, very often with *only* or *barely*: *We've only scratched the surface.* It can sound humble (admitting how much is left) or exciting (promising much more to discover). *That doesn't even scratch the surface* means something is far from enough.
entries.pattern: only / barely scratch the surface (of something)
examples: We spent a week in Japan, but we only **scratched the surface** of what the country has to offer.
The new money is welcome, but it barely **scratches the surface** of what the city's roads need.
Our intro class only **scratched the surface** of statistics, so I'm taking the advanced one now.

drill.sentence: I've read three books about the Civil War, but I feel like I've only {{scratched the surface}}.
drill.hint: dealt with only a tiny part of a huge subject

entries.related: *the tip of the iceberg* — a small visible part of a much bigger problem; *skim* — read quickly without detail; *dig deeper* — the opposite, look more closely.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To make a special effort to do something, especially to help someone, even when it is inconvenient for you.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, thank-you notes and reviews, usually followed by *to* + verb: *She went out of her way to help us.* It is warm praise when someone helps. It can also describe a deliberate effort with a negative aim: *He goes out of his way to avoid me.*
entries.pattern: go out of your way to do something
examples: Our neighbor **went out of his way** to shovel our driveway every morning while I was in the hospital.
The waiter **went out of his way** to find a gluten-free dessert for my daughter.
Ever since our argument, my coworker **goes out of her way** to avoid me in the hallway.

drill.sentence: The bus driver {{went out of her way}} to drop the lost little boy off right in front of his house.
drill.hint: made a special effort, though it wasn't convenient (not *… the extra mile* or *… above and beyond*)

entries.related: *go the extra mile* — do more than is expected; *bend over backwards* — try extremely hard to help or please someone; *put yourself out* — accept inconvenience to help someone.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To avoid attracting attention to yourself or your activities.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and news, often after a scandal or a mistake, or for privacy or safety. It is neutral and can sound wise or slightly suspicious, depending on context. The opposite, *a high profile*, means being well known or very visible.
examples: After the embarrassing video went viral, the coach **kept a low profile** for a few weeks.
Many celebrities **keep a low profile** on vacation, with hats, sunglasses and no social media.
As the new guy at the office, I'm **keeping a low profile** until I understand how things work.

drill.sentence: After her messy breakup became gossip all over campus, Tara {{kept a low profile}} and skipped most parties that semester.
drill.hint: avoided attention (not *lay low* or *stayed under the radar*)

entries.related: *lie low* — hide or avoid attention for a while, often to avoid trouble; *stay under the radar* — avoid being noticed; *in the spotlight* — the opposite, getting a lot of attention.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To watch someone or something closely so that you always know what they are doing or what is happening.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, news and work, with people, prices, competitors or situations as objects: *keep tabs on the kids*, *keep tabs on spending*. It is informal and neutral, but about people it can suggest monitoring or mild suspicion. *Keep close tabs on* stresses the attention.
entries.pattern: keep (close) tabs on someone / something
examples: Some parents use an app to **keep tabs on** where their teenagers are.
I **keep tabs on** flight prices for a month before I book anything.
Detectives have been **keeping close tabs on** the suspect since he was released.

drill.sentence: My grandmother lives alone, so my uncle calls every evening to {{keep tabs on}} her.
drill.hint: monitor how she's doing (not *… an eye on* or *check (in) on*)

entries.related: *keep an eye on someone* — watch someone, often to protect them; *keep track of* — follow information or numbers; *check up on someone* — make sure someone is OK or behaving.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To act cleverly and make the right decisions so that you get the result you want.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, usually in a conditional: *If you play your cards right, …* It often encourages someone or hints at a possible reward, sometimes playfully in dating. The possessive changes with the subject.
entries.pattern: if you play your cards right, …
examples: **If you play your cards right**, you could be managing this store within a year.
She **played her cards right** in the negotiation and got a higher salary and an extra week off.
"Can I get a second date?" "**Play your cards right** and maybe."

drill.sentence: The landlord likes you, so if you {{play your cards right}}, he might lower the rent.
drill.hint: act cleverly to get what you want — a game image

entries.related: *make the right moves* — plainer; *hold all the cards* — have all the advantages; *blow it* — informal, lose a good chance by acting badly.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To do the things you tell other people they should do, instead of giving advice that you do not follow yourself.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, parenting and commentary, often in the negative as criticism: *He doesn't practice what he preaches.* It is also used as praise for someone who is consistent. In American English the verb is spelled *practice*; British English uses *practise*.
examples: My dentist tells everyone to floss, and she **practices what she preaches**: her teeth are perfect.
It's hard to take money advice from a friend who doesn't **practice what he preaches**.
The CEO told everyone to cut costs and then bought a private jet; he clearly doesn't **practice what he preaches**.

drill.sentence: Our coach yells at us for eating junk food, but he has a soda in his hand at every game. He should {{practice what he preaches}}.
drill.hint: follow his own advice (not *walk the walk*)

entries.related: *walk the walk* — act in line with your words; *lead by example* — show others how to behave by doing it yourself; *a hypocrite* — someone whose actions contradict their words.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To do the same job or live the same kind of life as someone, usually a parent or relative, who did it before you.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, biographies and news about careers and families: *She followed in her father's footsteps and became a doctor.* The standard form keeps *in*. It is neutral to admiring and can also refer to a mentor or a famous person you want to imitate.
entries.pattern: follow in someone's footsteps
examples: Sofia **followed in her mother's footsteps** and became a nurse at the same hospital.
My dad hoped I'd **follow in his footsteps** and take over the farm, but I moved to the city.
Thousands of young girls picked up a tennis racket, hoping to **follow in Serena Williams's footsteps**.

drill.sentence: Both of Ray's parents were firefighters, so nobody was surprised when he {{followed in their footsteps}}.
drill.hint: took up the same career as them (keep the preposition)

entries.related: *a chip off the old block* — a child who is very similar to a parent; *carry on the family tradition* — continue what your family has always done; *pave the way* — make it easier for others to follow later.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Behaving as politely and correctly as possible, usually to make a good impression or because someone important is watching.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, especially with children, guests and new situations: *Be on your best behavior at Grandma's.* It often suggests that the good behavior is temporary or a little forced. American English spells it *behavior*; British English writes *behaviour*.
entries.pattern: be on your best behavior
examples: The kids were **on their best behavior** at the restaurant because they were hoping for dessert.
Everyone at the plant was **on their best behavior** this week while the new owner was visiting.
When I met my girlfriend's parents for the first time, I was **on my best behavior** all weekend.

drill.sentence: My nephew is usually wild, but when Santa visited his class, he was {{on his best behavior}}.
drill.hint: acting as politely as possible (not *good as gold*)

entries.related: *mind your manners* — be polite, often said to children; *good as gold* — very well-behaved, about children; *put your best foot forward* — try to make a good impression.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Crazy or very foolish; also, extremely worried, upset or bored, as in *out of your mind with worry*.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation. *Are you out of your mind?* is a strong reaction to a crazy idea and can sound rude; *out of my mind with worry* describes intense emotion. As an intensifier after an adjective, *bored / scared out of my mind* means extremely bored or scared.
entries.pattern: be out of your mind (with worry / grief); bored / scared out of your mind
examples: You want to quit your job and sail around the world? Are you **out of your mind**?
When our daughter didn't come home until three a.m., we were **out of our minds** with worry.
I was **bored out of my mind** during the three-hour safety training.

drill.sentence: You paid nine hundred dollars for a pair of sneakers? You must be {{out of your mind}}!
drill.hint: completely crazy (not *nuts* or *off your rocker*)

entries.related: *lose your mind* — become crazy or extremely stressed; *off your rocker* — informal, crazy; *at your wit's end* — so worried or frustrated that you don't know what to do.

entries.term: stick out like a sore thumb
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be very noticeable because it is different from everything or everyone around it and does not fit in.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, usually about people, clothes or buildings that look out of place: *In my suit, I stuck out like a sore thumb.* It is informal and usually mildly negative or self-mocking. *Stand out* is the neutral verb and is often positive.
examples: I showed up to the beach party in jeans and boots and **stuck out like a sore thumb**.
The glass tower **sticks out like a sore thumb** among the old brick buildings on Main Street.
As the only tourist in the tiny fishing village, my brother **stuck out like a sore thumb**.

drill.sentence: Everyone else wore black to the funeral, so my aunt's bright pink dress {{stuck out like a sore thumb}}.
drill.hint: was very noticeable and out of place — an injured-finger image

entries.related: *stand out* — be noticeable, often in a good way; *out of place* — not belonging; *a fish out of water* — someone who feels uncomfortable in a new situation.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Someone who feels awkward and uncomfortable because they are in an unfamiliar situation or surroundings.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, reviews and film descriptions, usually after *be* or *feel like*: *I felt like a fish out of water.* It describes the person's discomfort, not just how they look to others. Film and TV writers use *a fish-out-of-water story* for a plot about someone in a strange new world.
entries.pattern: be / feel like a fish out of water
examples: As a city kid at summer camp in the woods, I felt like **a fish out of water**.
My dad is **a fish out of water** at fancy restaurants; he just wants a burger.
The movie is a classic **fish-out-of-water** comedy about a New York lawyer who moves to a tiny farm town.

drill.sentence: Grace was the only accountant at the poetry reading, and she felt like {{a fish out of water}} all night.
drill.hint: someone awkward in a strange setting — an animal image

entries.related: *out of your element* — in a situation you are not used to; *in your element* — the opposite, comfortable and good at it; *stick out like a sore thumb* — look obviously different.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be good at expressing yourself in speech or writing, in a clear, clever or persuasive way.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and compliments, often with *really*: *She really has a way with words.* It is praise, but it can be mildly ironic about someone who talks smoothly to persuade. The frame also works with other nouns: *a way with kids*, *a way with animals*.
entries.pattern: have a way with words / kids / animals
examples: Your grandfather **had a way with words**; his letters still make me cry.
The best salespeople **have a way with words** that makes you trust them right away.
My daughter **has a way with words** — her teacher entered her poem in a state contest.

drill.sentence: Nobody gave a better toast at the wedding than Uncle Raj; he really {{has a way with words}}.
drill.hint: is good at expressing himself (not *has the gift of gab*)

entries.related: *have the gift of gab* — informal American, talk easily and persuasively, sometimes too much; *eloquent* — more formal; *at a loss for words* — the opposite, unable to say anything.

entries.term: know something like the back of your hand
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To know a place or a thing extremely well, in every detail.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, usually about places, routes, neighborhoods or something you use every day: *I know this city like the back of my hand.* It suggests long, close familiarity. The object goes after *know*, and the possessive matches the subject.
entries.pattern: know something like the back of your hand
examples: I grew up in Chicago, so I **know** the city **like the back of my hand**.
Ask Grandpa for directions — he **knows** these back roads **like the back of his hand**.
She's read *Pride and Prejudice* so many times that she **knows it like the back of her hand**.

drill.sentence: Mia has walked this trail every morning for twenty years; she {{knows it like the back of her hand}}.
drill.hint: is extremely familiar with it — a body image (not *inside out* or *by heart*)

mistake.wrong: I know this neighborhood like the palm of my hand.
mistake.right: I know this neighborhood like the back of my hand.
mistake.why: Several languages use the palm (Spanish *como la palma de la mano*), but in English it is always *the back of your hand*.

entries.related: *know something inside out* — know it thoroughly; *know something by heart* — have it memorized; *second nature* — something you do automatically.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Unwilling to change your habits, routines or opinions, usually because you have had them for a long time.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, often about older people or long habits, and often with *very* or *a little*: *My dad is very set in his ways.* It is mildly critical but often affectionate. It follows *be*, *get* or *become*: *You get set in your ways when you live alone.*
entries.pattern: be / get set in your ways
examples: My grandfather is so **set in his ways** that he still pays for groceries with a check.
After fifteen years of living alone, I've gotten a little **set in my ways**.
Some longtime employees were too **set in their ways** to learn the new scheduling system.

drill.sentence: My dad won't use GPS because he likes his paper maps. He's very {{set in his ways}}.
drill.hint: unwilling to change his habits (not *stuck …* or *old-fashioned*)

entries.related: *a creature of habit* — someone who likes routine, less critical; *old habits die hard* — habits are hard to change; *stuck in a rut* — trapped in a boring routine you want to escape.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Someone who likes routine and always does the same things in the same way.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, often about yourself with a smile: *I'm a creature of habit.* It is usually neutral or affectionate, less critical than *set in your ways*. It typically follows *be* and describes daily routines, food choices or favorite seats.
examples: I'm **a creature of habit**: same coffee, same table, same time every morning.
Our cat is **a creature of habit** and starts meowing at six sharp for breakfast.
Burglars know that most people are **creatures of habit** and leave home at the same time every day.

drill.sentence: Dad has sat in the same booth at the same diner every Saturday for twenty years. He's {{a creature of habit}}.
drill.hint: someone who loves routine (not *set in his ways*)

entries.related: *set in your ways* — unwilling to change, more critical; *stuck in a rut* — bored by routine; *like clockwork* — happening regularly and exactly on time.

entries.term: you can't teach an old dog new tricks
entries.label: saying
entries.meaning: It is hard for people who are older, or who have done something one way for a long time, to learn new skills or change their habits.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, often humorously about yourself or older relatives, especially with technology. It is also often challenged: *Who says you can't teach an old dog new tricks?* Calling another person an *old dog* to their face can sound rude, so it is safer to use about yourself.
examples: My dad still can't send a photo from his phone — **you can't teach an old dog new tricks**.
At seventy-two, my mom learned to swim. So much for **you can't teach an old dog new tricks**!
Grandpa joked that **you can't teach an old dog new tricks**, then beat us all at the video game.

drill.sentence: My uncle still won't learn to cook anything but eggs. He just shrugs and says {{you can't teach an old dog new tricks}}.
drill.hint: older people don't change their habits — an animal saying

entries.related: *set in your ways* — unwilling to change; *old habits die hard* — habits are hard to break; *it's never too late to learn* — the opposite view.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Stuck in a boring routine or situation that does not change or progress, and finding it hard to get out.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about work, relationships and life in general, usually with *be stuck* or *get*: *I feel like I'm stuck in a rut.* It suggests boredom and a lack of progress, often with a wish for change. It fits both personal and professional contexts.
entries.pattern: be / get (stuck) in a rut
examples: I've had the same job for eight years, and I feel like I'm stuck **in a rut**.
Their marriage was **in a rut**, so they started taking salsa classes together.
The team's offense has been **in a rut** for weeks, scoring fewer than twenty points a game.

drill.sentence: Every day it's work, dinner, TV, bed. I need a new hobby — I'm totally {{in a rut}}.
drill.hint: stuck in a dull routine (not *in a slump*)

entries.related: *in a slump* — in a period of poor results or low mood; *the daily grind* — boring, tiring everyday work; *shake things up* — make changes to escape a routine.
entries.origin: A *rut* is a deep track worn into a dirt road by wheels, which is hard to steer out of.

entries.term: step out of your comfort zone
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To try something new or challenging that makes you a little nervous or uncomfortable, usually so that you can grow.
entries.usage: Very common in advice, education and motivational talk, often with *need to* or *push yourself to*. It is positive and encouraging. Common variants are *get out of your comfort zone* and *push someone out of their comfort zone*.
entries.pattern: step / get out of your comfort zone; push someone out of their comfort zone
examples: Joining the debate team really helped me **step out of my comfort zone**.
Traveling alone forced Ana to **step out of her comfort zone** and talk to strangers.
Good coaches push players to **step out of their comfort zone** in practice.

drill.sentence: I'm pretty shy, but I signed up for an improv class this fall to {{step out of my comfort zone}}.
drill.hint: do something new that makes me uneasy (not *get out of …*)

entries.related: *push yourself* — make yourself work harder; *take the plunge* — finally do something difficult or risky; *play it safe* — the opposite, avoid risk.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Practical, sensible and friendly, without acting as if you are more important than other people.
entries.usage: Very common praise in conversation and interviews, often about famous or successful people who behave normally: *She's so down-to-earth.* It is hyphenated before a noun (*a down-to-earth guy*) and often written without hyphens after *be*. It can also describe practical advice or an approach.
examples: For a famous actress, she was surprisingly **down-to-earth** and chatted with us about her kids.
Our family doctor is a **down-to-earth** guy who explains everything in plain English.
I liked the book's **down-to-earth** advice on saving for a first home.

drill.sentence: Despite making millions, the quarterback is very {{down-to-earth}} and still drives his old pickup truck.
drill.hint: practical and friendly, not proud — a soil image (not *grounded* or *humble*)

entries.related: *grounded* — calm and sensible; *humble* — not proud; *stuck-up* — informal, the opposite: thinks they're better than others.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be very kind, generous and caring toward other people.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and in tributes, toasts and eulogies. It often follows a *but* that admits a flaw: *He's grumpy, but he has a heart of gold.* It is warm and affectionate, and it also appears as *with a heart of gold* after a noun.
entries.pattern: have a heart of gold; someone with a heart of gold
examples: Our neighbor looks tough, but he **has a heart of gold**; he fixes every kid's bike on the street for free.
At her funeral, everyone said Aunt Rosa **had a heart of gold**.
The cafeteria lady with **a heart of gold** always slipped extra cookies to the hungry kids.

drill.sentence: Everyone in town knows Mr. Lopez {{has a heart of gold}}; he gives free haircuts to kids before every school year.
drill.hint: is truly kind and generous — a precious-metal image

entries.related: *kindhearted* — kind and caring; *have a big heart* — be very generous; *heartless* — the opposite, cruel.

entries.term: the apple doesn't fall far from the tree
entries.label: saying
entries.meaning: Children usually have similar qualities, talents or faults to their parents.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, often with a knowing smile after describing a child: *Her son's a lawyer too — the apple doesn't fall far from the tree.* It can be a compliment or a criticism, depending on whether the shared trait is good or bad. *The apple never falls far from the tree* is a common variant.
examples: Her dad was a concert pianist, and now she's at Juilliard — **the apple doesn't fall far from the tree**.
Jake's always late, just like his father. **The apple doesn't fall far from the tree**.
Watching my daughter argue with the referee, I realized **the apple didn't fall far from the tree**.

drill.sentence: Sam's mom loves cooking, and now he's in culinary school. {{The apple doesn't fall far from the tree}}.
drill.hint: children turn out like their parents — a fruit saying

entries.related: *a chip off the old block* — a child who is very like a parent; *like father, like son* — a son is similar to his father; *run in the family* — be common in a family.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be common among members of a family, as a trait, talent, illness or habit passed from one generation to the next.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and in medical contexts: *Heart disease runs in my family.* The subject is the trait, not the person, and *the family* often becomes *my / our family*. It is neutral and works for talents, looks, illnesses and habits.
entries.pattern: something runs in the / your family
examples: Red hair **runs in our family**; my grandmother, my mom and my son all have it.
Because diabetes **runs in his family**, Raj gets his blood sugar checked every year.
Both of her brothers are musicians, so talent clearly **runs in the family**.

drill.sentence: My dad and grandpa both lost their hair before forty. Baldness {{runs in the family}}, I guess.
drill.hint: is passed down among relatives

entries.related: *hereditary* — passed down genetically, more formal; *the apple doesn't fall far from the tree* — children are like their parents; *in your genes* — a natural part of you because of your parents.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To get married.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, news and celebrity reporting, often with *with* + partner: *He tied the knot with his college sweetheart.* It is informal and cheerful, and very frequent in headlines. It refers to the wedding itself, not to being married.
entries.pattern: tie the knot (with someone)
examples: After dating for seven years, Maya and Chris finally **tied the knot** last June.
My parents **tied the knot** at city hall with just two friends as witnesses.
More couples are waiting until their thirties to **tie the knot**, a new survey shows.

drill.sentence: Jen and Marcus met in kindergarten, and twenty-five years later they {{tied the knot}} in the same small town.
drill.hint: got married — a rope image (not *got hitched*)

entries.related: *get hitched* — informal, also means get married; *walk down the aisle* — get married, focusing on the ceremony; *pop the question* — ask someone to marry you.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To betray someone who trusts you, usually by secretly doing something that harms them.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, workplace talk and news about friendships, business and sports. It is strong and emotional, often said by the person who was betrayed: *She stabbed me in the back.* The noun is *a stab in the back*, and a *backstabber* is someone who does this often.
examples: I helped him get the job, and then he **stabbed me in the back** by taking credit for my work.
Fans felt the star had **stabbed** the team **in the back** when he signed with their biggest rival.
Reality shows are full of contestants who smile at each other and then **stab each other in the back**.

drill.sentence: I told my best friend I liked Daniel, and she {{stabbed me in the back}} by asking him out the next day.
drill.hint: betrayed me — a knife image

entries.related: *betray* — plainer; *throw someone under the bus* — blame someone to save yourself; *double-cross* — cheat someone you were working with.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To imagine how you would feel or what you would do if you were in someone else's situation.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and advice, often as a request for empathy: *Put yourself in my shoes.* It also appears with *try to* and in *if you put yourself in their shoes*. *Be in someone's shoes* means actually being in their situation: *I wouldn't want to be in his shoes.*
entries.pattern: put yourself in someone's shoes; be in someone's shoes
examples: Before you get angry at the waiter, **put yourself in his shoes** — he's serving twenty tables alone.
Good doctors try to **put themselves in their patients' shoes**.
**Put yourself in my shoes**: what would you do if your boss texted you every night at eleven?

drill.sentence: I know you're upset that she canceled, but {{put yourself in her shoes}} — her mom just went into the hospital.
drill.hint: imagine her situation — a footwear image

entries.related: *see things from someone's point of view* — plainer; *walk a mile in someone's shoes* — fully experience someone's life before judging them; *empathize with someone* — more formal.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To persuade someone to do something they do not really want to do, often by pressing them.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, and very often used jokingly about something the speaker actually wants to do: *Another slice of pie? Well, if you twist my arm …* It can also describe real pressure, and then it is mildly critical. *Twist a few arms* means pressuring several people to get support.
examples: I didn't want to go to karaoke night, but my roommate **twisted my arm**.
"Want to come to Hawaii with us?" "Well, if you **twist my arm** …"
The PTA president had to **twist** a few **arms** to find enough parents for the bake sale.

drill.sentence: My sister hates hiking, but I {{twisted her arm}} and she came with us to the Grand Canyon.
drill.hint: persuaded her against her will — a wrestling image (not *talked her into it*)

entries.related: *talk someone into something* — persuade someone, neutral; *pressure someone* — plainer; *need no persuading* — already want to do it.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To tease someone by telling them something untrue as a joke, hoping they will believe it.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, often as a question when you suspect a joke: *Are you pulling my leg?* It is friendly and playful, never cruel. *I'm just pulling your leg* means *I'm only joking.*
entries.pattern: pull someone's leg; be pulling someone's leg
examples: Relax, I'm just **pulling your leg** — the test isn't really tomorrow.
When Grandpa said he'd once met Elvis, we thought he was **pulling our leg**, but he had a photo to prove it.
"They're closing every coffee shop in town." "You're **pulling my leg**, right?"

drill.sentence: When my brother told me he'd won a trip to the moon, I knew he was {{pulling my leg}}.
drill.hint: playfully fooling me (not *kidding* or *messing with me*)

entries.related: *kid someone* — joke with someone; *mess with someone* — informal, tease or trick someone; *have someone on* — British, the same.

entries.term: a taste of your own medicine
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The same unpleasant treatment that you have given to other people, now given back to you.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and stories, usually with *give someone* or *get*: *Let's give him a taste of his own medicine.* It suggests the person deserves it, so it often sounds satisfied or a little vengeful. The possessive matches the person: *a taste of her own medicine*.
entries.pattern: give someone / get a taste of their own medicine
examples: My brother always hid my phone, so I hid his for a day to give him **a taste of his own medicine**.
The bully got **a taste of his own medicine** when the new kid stood up to him in front of everyone.
The team that loved to run up the score finally got **a taste of its own medicine** in a fifty-to-nothing loss.

drill.sentence: My cousin always shows up an hour late, so this time I made him wait for me to give him {{a taste of his own medicine}}.
drill.hint: the same bad treatment he gives others — a pharmacy image

entries.related: *get what's coming to you* — get the punishment you deserve; *tit for tat* — doing the same harm in return; *turn the tables* — reverse a situation so you have the advantage.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Secretly, without the person knowing, usually doing something they would not like.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about gossip, betrayal and secret plans: *They were talking about me behind my back.* It usually follows verbs like *talk*, *complain* or *laugh*. *Go behind someone's back* means doing something without asking a person who should have been asked.
entries.pattern: do something behind someone's back; go behind someone's back
examples: I can't believe my best friend was complaining about me **behind my back**.
Instead of asking his manager, Tom **went behind her back** and emailed the director directly.
Teenagers who sneak out **behind their parents' backs** usually get caught eventually.

drill.sentence: My sister borrowed my car {{behind my back}} and returned it with an empty tank.
drill.hint: secretly, while I didn't know — a body image

entries.related: *behind closed doors* — in private, not in public; *on the sly* — secretly, informal; *to someone's face* — the opposite, directly and openly.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To not tell someone about something important that they should know or want to know.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and news, usually as a complaint: *They kept us in the dark.* It is often passive (*We were kept in the dark*) and often takes *about*. The opposite is *keep someone in the loop*.
entries.pattern: keep someone in the dark (about something); be kept in the dark
examples: The airline **kept** passengers **in the dark** for three hours about why the flight was delayed.
My parents **kept me in the dark** about their money problems until I was in college.
Employees say they were **kept in the dark** about the merger until they read about it in the news.

drill.sentence: Please don't {{keep me in the dark}} — if the test results are bad, I want to know.
drill.hint: hide information from me (not *… out of the loop*)

entries.related: *keep someone in the loop* — the opposite, keep them informed; *out of the loop* — not included in information; *keep something under wraps* — keep it secret.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To receive official permission to start or continue a project or plan.
entries.usage: Common in business, news and entertainment: *The project got the green light.* Related forms are *give something the green light* and the verb *greenlight*, frequent in film and TV news: *The studio greenlit a sequel.* It is neutral and fits both conversation and writing.
entries.pattern: get / give someone the green light (to do something)
examples: After two years of planning, the new children's hospital finally **got the green light**.
We **got the green light** from the city to turn our garage into a small studio.
The studio **gave the green light** to a third movie after the second one made a billion dollars.

drill.sentence: Six weeks after my knee surgery, I finally {{got the green light}} from my doctor to start running again.
drill.hint: received permission — a traffic image (not *the go-ahead* or *the all-clear*)

entries.related: *get the go-ahead* — same, plainer; *get the all-clear* — be told it is safe, often by a doctor; *put something on hold* — the opposite, stop it for now.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To criticize, tease or cause problems for someone, either seriously or in a friendly, joking way.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, and the tone depends on context: friendly teasing (*My friends gave me a hard time about my haircut*) or real trouble (*The landlord is giving us a hard time*). It often takes *about* or *for*. *Don't give me a hard time* means *don't make this harder for me*.
entries.pattern: give someone a hard time (about / for something)
examples: My brothers still **give me a hard time** about the day I drove into the mailbox.
The agent at the check-in desk **gave us a hard time** because one bag was a pound over the limit.
Please don't **give your sister a hard time** — she's having a rough week.

drill.sentence: When I showed up in a Yankees cap at the Red Sox game, everyone around me {{gave me a hard time}}.
drill.hint: teased and criticized me (not *… grief*)

entries.related: *give someone grief* — similar, informal; *tease* — make fun of someone playfully; *go easy on someone* — the opposite, treat them gently.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To try as hard as you can to do something, even if success is not certain.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and encouragement before a difficult attempt: *Just give it your best shot.* It suggests that effort matters more than the result. *I'll give it my best shot* is a modest promise, and *give it a shot* simply means *try*.
examples: You may not win the scholarship, but **give it your best shot** and see what happens.
I've never baked a wedding cake before, but I'll **give it my best shot**.
The team **gave it their best shot**, but the champions were simply too strong.

drill.sentence: The audition is tomorrow. Don't worry about the other singers — just go in there and {{give it your best shot}}.
drill.hint: try as hard as you can (not *… your all* or *go for it*)

entries.related: *give it a shot* — try, less intense; *give it your all* — use all your energy; *go for it* — informal encouragement to try.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To cost more money than you can afford, or to use up all your money.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and advertising, usually in the negative: *It won't break the bank.* It reassures people that something is affordable. The subject is the thing or plan that costs money: *A weekend trip doesn't have to break the bank.*
examples: You can eat really well in this city without **breaking the bank**.
A small birthday party at the park won't **break the bank**.
Fixing the roof now is cheaper than waiting; replacing the whole thing later would really **break the bank**.

drill.sentence: We wanted a nice anniversary dinner, but something that wouldn't {{break the bank}}.
drill.hint: cost far too much (not *cost a fortune* or *cost an arm and a leg*)

entries.related: *cost an arm and a leg* — be very expensive; *on a shoestring* — with very little money; *affordable* — plainer.
entries.origin: From gambling: a player who *breaks the bank* wins more money than the casino has available at that table.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To have just enough money to pay for the things you need, such as rent, food and bills.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and news about money, work and the cost of living, often with *struggle to*, *barely* or *hard to*: *Many families are struggling to make ends meet.* It describes getting by, not living comfortably. The form is fixed, and *ends* is always plural.
entries.pattern: (struggle to / barely) make ends meet
examples: Since prices went up, a lot of families are struggling to **make ends meet**.
When my parents were first married, they worked three jobs between them to **make ends meet**.
I drive for a delivery app on weekends to help **make ends meet**.

drill.sentence: After the factory cut her hours, Maria took a second job at a diner just to {{make ends meet}}.
drill.hint: pay her basic costs (not *get by* or *pay the bills*)

entries.related: *get by* — manage with what you have; *live paycheck to paycheck* — spend all your income before the next pay arrives; *scrape by* — survive with very little money.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Very common and easy to find, and therefore not special or valuable.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation, usually after *be*: *Coffee shops are a dime a dozen here.* It often sets up a contrast with something rare: *Good ideas are a dime a dozen; good execution isn't.* A *dime* is a ten-cent coin; British English says *ten a penny*.
examples: Pizza places are **a dime a dozen** in this neighborhood, but good ones are rare.
In a city like Los Angeles, aspiring actors are **a dime a dozen**.
A friend who'll help you move on a Sunday isn't **a dime a dozen** — hold on to him.

drill.sentence: Don't pay extra for that phone charger at the airport; they're {{a dime a dozen}} at any gas station.
drill.hint: very common and cheap — a coin image (not *ten a penny*)

entries.related: *ten a penny* — the British version; *run-of-the-mill* — ordinary; *one in a million* — the opposite, very rare and special.

entries.term: put all your eggs in one basket
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To risk everything on a single plan, investment or opportunity, so that you could lose everything if it fails.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and in money or career advice, usually as a warning in the negative: *Don't put all your eggs in one basket.* It fits investing, job hunting and business. The idea behind it is *diversify*.
examples: Apply to several colleges — don't **put all your eggs in one basket**.
The town **put all its eggs in one basket** with the steel mill, and when it closed, half the jobs disappeared.
Financial planners warn against **putting all your eggs in one basket** by holding only your employer's stock.

drill.sentence: Lisa grew nothing but strawberries on her farm, so the hailstorm wiped her out. She'd {{put all her eggs in one basket}}.
drill.hint: risked everything on a single option — a farm image

entries.related: *diversify* — spread money or risk across different things; *hedge your bets* — protect yourself by supporting more than one option; *go all in* — risk everything, from poker.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To have sudden great luck or success, often by finding or winning exactly what you wanted.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and news, about winning money and, even more often, about lucky finds: *We hit the jackpot with this apartment.* It is informal and enthusiastic. The literal sense is winning the top prize in a lottery or on a slot machine.
examples: We **hit the jackpot** at the flea market: a whole box of old vinyl records for ten dollars.
A retired teacher in Ohio **hit the jackpot**, winning two million dollars in the state lottery.
Our town **hit the jackpot** when a big carmaker chose it for its new factory.

drill.sentence: After looking at twenty apartments, we finally {{hit the jackpot}}: big windows, low rent and a friendly landlord.
drill.hint: had amazing luck — a casino image (not *struck gold* or *lucked out*)

entries.related: *strike gold* — find something very valuable; *luck out* — informal American, be lucky; *a windfall* — an unexpected amount of money.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To pay the bill for everyone, especially in a restaurant or bar, or to pay the cost of something for someone else.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and news: *My uncle picked up the tab for dinner.* *Tab* is an informal word for a bill, especially in a restaurant or bar. In news it also means paying on behalf of others: *Taxpayers will pick up the tab.*
entries.pattern: pick up the tab (for something)
examples: We tried to split the check, but my boss insisted on **picking up the tab**.
The bride's parents **picked up the tab** for the whole wedding.
If the new arena loses money, local taxpayers will have to **pick up the tab**.

drill.sentence: It's your birthday, so put your wallet away — I'm {{picking up the tab}} tonight.
drill.hint: paying the bill for everyone (not *buying* or *treating*)

entries.related: *foot the bill* — pay, often for something expensive; *it's on me* — I'll pay; *go Dutch* — each person pays for themselves.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Just before it is too late, at the last possible moment.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and storytelling, especially in dramatic or relieved accounts: *The ambulance arrived in the nick of time.* It is often preceded by *just*. It stresses a lucky escape, such as a rescue or a deadline met with seconds to spare.
examples: We got to the gate **in the nick of time**, just as they were closing the door.
A lifeguard reached the struggling swimmer **in the nick of time**.
I filed my tax return **just in the nick of time**, at 11:58 p.m. on April fifteenth.

drill.sentence: I pulled the cookies out of the oven {{in the nick of time}}, seconds before they started to burn.
drill.hint: barely soon enough (not *just in …* or *at the last minute*)

entries.related: *just in time* — plainer; *at the eleventh hour* — at the last moment, often about decisions; *with seconds to spare* — barely in time.

entries.term: in the blink of an eye
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Extremely quickly; in a very short moment.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, storytelling and writing, often about sudden changes or how fast time passes: *The kids grew up in the blink of an eye.* It is vivid and slightly emotional. It works at the start or the end of a sentence.
examples: One wrong step on the ice, and **in the blink of an eye** I was flat on my back.
Summer vacation went by **in the blink of an eye**.
The concert sold out **in the blink of an eye**, and resale prices tripled.

drill.sentence: Enjoy these years with your baby — she'll be leaving for college {{in the blink of an eye}}.
drill.hint: incredibly fast (not *before you know it* or *in no time*)

entries.related: *in a flash* — very quickly; *before you know it* — sooner than you expect; *in a heartbeat* — immediately and without hesitating.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: All day and all night, without stopping.
entries.usage: Common in news and conversation about work, care and services: *Nurses watched him around the clock.* It works after a verb and, with hyphens, before a noun: *around-the-clock care*. British English often says *round the clock*.
entries.pattern: work / be open around the clock; around-the-clock + noun
examples: After his surgery, nurses checked on him **around the clock**.
Crews worked **around the clock** to repair the bridge before the holiday weekend.
Newborns need **around-the-clock** care, so new parents rarely sleep more than three hours.

drill.sentence: This diner is open {{around the clock}}, so you can get pancakes at three in the morning.
drill.hint: twenty-four hours a day — a time-telling image (not *twenty-four seven*)

entries.related: *24/7* — informal, all the time; *nonstop* — without a break; *day and night* — constantly.

entries.label: saying
entries.meaning: It is better to do something or arrive late than not to do it at all.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, often as a cheerful excuse or a friendly reply when someone apologizes for being late: *Better late than never!* It can also be mildly sarcastic when something should have happened long ago. It is usually a short comment on its own.
examples: I finally got my driver's license at thirty-five. **Better late than never**!
"Sorry I forgot your birthday — here's your card." "Hey, **better late than never**."
The city finally fixed the pothole on our street after three years. **Better late than never**, I suppose.

drill.sentence: Grandma finished her college degree at seventy-one. As she put it, {{better late than never}}.
drill.hint: a delay beats not doing it at all — a short saying

entries.related: *it's never too late* — you can still start something; *about time* — said when something should have happened earlier; *too little, too late* — not enough and not soon enough to help.

entries.term: in the heat of the moment
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: While feeling a strong emotion, such as anger or excitement, without stopping to think.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, apologies and news, usually to explain or excuse something said or done: *I said things in the heat of the moment that I regret.* It implies the action was not planned and may not reflect real feelings. *On the spur of the moment* is different: it means a sudden, unplanned decision, without strong emotion.
examples: I'm sorry I yelled at you; I said some things **in the heat of the moment**.
The player was thrown out of the game after shoving a referee **in the heat of the moment**.
**In the heat of the moment**, it's easy to send an angry email you'll regret the next day.

drill.sentence: It was a stupid fight, and I know Dad didn't mean what he said {{in the heat of the moment}}.
drill.hint: while emotions were running high (not *on the spur …*)

entries.related: *on the spur of the moment* — suddenly, without planning; *lose your temper* — become angry; *act on impulse* — do something without thinking.

entries.term: on the spur of the moment
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Suddenly, without planning or thinking about it in advance.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and stories about trips, purchases and decisions: *We drove to the coast on the spur of the moment.* Before a noun it is hyphenated: *a spur-of-the-moment decision*. It sounds neutral or positive, unlike *in the heat of the moment*, which suggests strong emotion.
entries.pattern: on the spur of the moment; a spur-of-the-moment + noun
examples: We didn't plan the road trip — we left **on the spur of the moment** after work on Friday.
I bought the concert tickets **on the spur of the moment**, and it was the best night of the year.
Their wedding in Las Vegas was a **spur-of-the-moment** decision.

drill.sentence: Grandpa decided {{on the spur of the moment}} to take us all out for ice cream after dinner.
drill.hint: suddenly, with no planning (not *on a whim*, *on impulse* or *out of the blue*)

mistake.wrong: We booked the trip in the spur of the moment.
mistake.right: We booked the trip on the spur of the moment.
mistake.why: The fixed phrase uses *on*; learners often say *in*, probably by analogy with *in the heat of the moment*.

entries.related: *on a whim* — because of a sudden wish; *on impulse* — without thinking first; *in the heat of the moment* — while feeling a strong emotion.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Going to happen very soon.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, ads and news about seasons, holidays and events: *Summer is just around the corner.* It often creates excitement or a sense of urgency. It also has a literal meaning, *very close by*, so context shows which one is meant; *right around the corner* works the same way.
examples: With spring **just around the corner**, the garden centers are already busy.
Finals are **just around the corner**, so the library is packed every night.
Some economists warn that a recession could be **just around the corner**.

drill.sentence: Thanksgiving is {{just around the corner}}, and I still haven't ordered the turkey.
drill.hint: coming very soon — a street image (not *right …*)

entries.related: *right around the corner* — same; *on the horizon* — likely to happen in the future; *any day now* — very soon.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Certain to happen sooner or later, even though nobody knows exactly when.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and news, usually as *It's only a matter of time before / until …*. It often predicts something bad, like an accident or getting caught, but it can be positive too. The tone is confident and a little ominous; *just a matter of time* is a common variant.
entries.pattern: it's only a matter of time before / until …
examples: With so much traffic on such a narrow road, it was **only a matter of time** before someone got hurt.
She's so talented that it's **only a matter of time** until a big label signs her.
Geologists say it's **only a matter of time** before the volcano erupts again.

drill.sentence: My son leaves his bike unlocked outside every store. It's {{only a matter of time}} before someone steals it.
drill.hint: bound to happen eventually (not *just …*)

entries.related: *sooner or later* — at some time in the future; *bound to happen* — certain to happen; *it's just a matter of time* — same, slightly more casual.
